speaker: FAA / CBP / Army (incident); Reps. Larsen and colleagues
venue: El Paso airspace closures (Feb 11 and Feb 27, 2026)
quote: Our heads are exploding over the news.
points: A counter-drone laser fired near Fort Bliss without FAA coordination; the FAA closed El Paso airspace for more than seven hours (Feb 11).
On Feb 27 the military used a laser to shoot down a CBP drone and the FAA closed more airspace nearby.
The FAA lifted restrictions after the Army agreed to more safety testing.
um_relevance: Even in a remote border setting, directed energy near civil airspace triggered FAA shutdowns and congressional anger. That reinforces the political value of a low-collateral physical capture effector, and the need to coordinate any airborne interceptor with the FAA.

speaker: Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor
quote: Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel
points: First military use of AMP-HEL against cartel-linked drones on the border (3 engaged).
~8,000 service members deployed under JTF-SB since March 2025.

DoW figures reported by Fox News: 378 cartel drones detected from Aug 22 to late Sept 2026; 75 turned back, 15 engaged, 1 captured. The military also reported taking down about 100 suspected cartel drones in August.
um_relevance: The border is a homeland C-UAS mission with real volume (hundreds of drones a month), remote terrain, and RF-evasive cartel tactics. A recoverable interceptor with its own sensors fits, and JTF-SB is a reachable operational customer through NORTHCOM and JIATF-401.

speaker: Lt. Cmdr. Lauren Cole
role: Deputy Director of Public Affairs, JTF-SB
quote: These narco-terrorist cartels are evolving in how they use drones
points: Cartels use drones for surveillance of US personnel, route reconnaissance and package transport, and keep changing tactics to avoid detection.
Systems in use include DroneBuster, Pitbull jammers, mobile and fixed detection, and kinetic and non-kinetic mitigation.
um_relevance: Cartels adapting to avoid RF detection and jamming is the scenario where onboard radar and EO/IR matter.

speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross; Brent Ingraham
quote: Countering against the threat of drones is both a warfighting and a homeland defense imperative.
points: Ingraham: "There isn't one answer to the drone threat."
Next: more IDIQ awards, allied marketplace access (Australia, Romania, 20+ countries), continued directed-energy pilots.
um_relevance: One year in, JIATF-401 is widening both vendor and buyer pools. Late entrants can still get on, but only with data.

speaker: JIATF-401
quote: (QRG) 37 C-sUAS systems commonly found in the US services today, with a common technical baseline for sensors, C2 and intercept against Group 1–3
points: Interceptors listed: Coyote, Anvil, Roadrunner, Bumblebee ('collision-interceptor'), Paladin, DroneHunter and others.
Fixed/semi-fixed: FS-LIDS, Pulsar, I-CsUAS, SUADS, CORIAN, EchoShield, KuRFS. Handheld: Dedrone Defender 2, DroneBuster IV, SMASH 2000L. DE: AMP-HEL, LOCUST, Leonidas.
C2: Lattice and FAAD C2 (MEDUSA also listed). The list is not all-inclusive.
um_relevance: The QRG is the de facto government shelf, and DroneHunter (capture) and Bumblebee (collision) are already on it. Getting UM into a future edition is a concrete milestone after characterization.

speaker: Brig. Gen. Matt Ross; Maj. Joe Amoroso
role: Director, JIATF-401; Deputy Chief of Strategic Initiatives, JIATF-401
quote: no single technology that resolves the drone threat
points: Framework: the 'Four Ps' (person, platform, process, payload) and 'Five Ds' (detect, deny, disrupt, defeat, discipline).
Treats kinetic defeat as a last resort at home and notes that private individuals generally may not shoot down drones.
um_relevance: Doctrine places physical defeat after detection, denial and disruption at home. UM's pitch should present capture as the controlled, low-collateral form of 'defeat' that applies where denial and disruption fail, such as against RF-silent drones.

speaker: Mike Torphy; Matt Whitehead; Charles Werner
role: FBI counter-UAS program lead; Director for emerging threats, White House NSC; Director, DroneResponders
venue: FedScoop: FBI drone training center demand outpaces capacity
quote: Bomb squads are expensive and to be good, you need to do it a lot. This is definitely true of counter-UAS.
points: World Cup 2026: 1,700 unauthorized drones detected, 700 seized, 400+ mitigation actions.
About 1,000 people trained over three years; 250 more mitigation officers planned by end of FY27.
Planning for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics is already under way (Torphy).
um_relevance: State and local mitigation will stay scarce and certification-gated through 2028. Near-term homeland demand runs through federal operators (FBI, DHS, DoD) who already hold authority.

speaker: Cmdr. Philip W. Rohlfing, USN
quote: (Analysis) About 60 SLTT personnel certified by June 2026 against a universe of 18,500+ agencies
points: The FBI NCUTC is the sole certifying authority; the first class (Nov 2025) was about 12 officers.
Recommends federally accredited state-delivered training on a NIMS-like model.
um_relevance: Confirms the SLTT market is years from scale. Treat it as a 2028+ upside, not a near-term revenue line.
